title: A Fountain Opened, a Shepherd Struck
summary: God promises a fountain that will wash the house of David and Jerusalem clean of sin and impurity, and he vows to remove idols and false prophecy from the land so completely that would-be prophets will deny they ever were one. Then the LORD summons a sword against his own shepherd; the flock scatters, and a remnant is brought through fire, refined, and bound to God again in covenant.
story: Chapter 12 ended with Jerusalem rescued from the nations and then mourning, as the people looked on the one they had pierced and grieved as for an only child. Chapter 13 answers that grief with cleansing. The tears of 12:10-14 are met by a fountain, and repentance is followed by the removal of everything that had corrupted Israel's worship: the idols that brought on the exile and the lying prophets who had soothed the people on the way there. Then the chapter turns sharply to the shepherd theme of chapters 9 to 11, where Israel's leaders had failed and a good shepherd had been rejected and valued at thirty pieces of silver. Now the shepherd himself is struck, by God's own order, and out of the scattering a purified people emerges. Chapter 14 will carry that remnant into the final day of the LORD.
historical:
This oracle belongs to the second burden of Zechariah (chapters 12 to 14), which carries no date. Those who hold that Zechariah himself wrote it place it in the later part of his ministry, in the early fifth century BC, when Judah was a small province of the Persian Empire with a rebuilt temple (finished in 515 BC) but no king. Many critical scholars date these chapters to the fifth or fourth century BC and attribute them to a later prophet in Zechariah's line. Either way, the first hearers lived after the exile, in a community that remembered why Jerusalem had fallen in 587 or 586 BC.

That memory explains the targets here. The prophets before the exile, especially Jeremiah and Ezekiel, had blamed the disaster on two things: idolatry and prophets who promised peace when there was no peace (Jeremiah 23; Ezekiel 13). After the return, overt worship of other gods seems to have faded in Judah, but prophecy itself was falling under suspicion. Nehemiah 6:10-14 records prophets hired to frighten Nehemiah, including a prophetess named Noadiah. Zechariah 13 looks toward a day when the whole sorry business of false prophecy is ended at the root.
cultural:
Several details draw on Israel's law and prophetic customs. The word for impurity in verse 1 is the term used for menstrual uncleanness and for the special water of cleansing mixed with the ashes of a red heifer in Numbers 19, which purified someone who had touched a corpse. A fountain opened for sin and impurity takes that ritual and makes it permanent and unlimited. Verse 3 applies the law of Deuteronomy 13 and 18, which required death for a prophet who spoke in God's name what God had not said, and which insisted that even a family member who enticed others to other gods must not be shielded. Here the parents themselves carry out the sentence, the ones who gave the prophet life. The verb for pierce is the same one used of the pierced one in 12:10, a deliberate echo.

The hairy cloak of verse 4 was the recognizable garment of a prophet; Elijah was known as a hairy man with a leather belt (2 Kings 1:8), and his cloak passed to Elisha. The disowning prophet of verse 5 borrows the words of Amos, who said he was a farmer and not a professional prophet, but uses them to lie. The wounds of verse 6, on the chest or literally between the hands, recall the self-cutting that marked ecstatic prophecy in the ancient Near East, as with the prophets of Baal who cut themselves on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:28). Caught with the scars, the man blames a brawl among friends.
literary: The chapter has two movements. Verses 1 to 6 are prose-like oracle held together by the repeated phrase on that day, which runs like a drumbeat through chapters 12 to 14 and binds them together. Verses 7 to 9 shift into poetry, with a direct address to a sword, a pair of commands (strike, and the sheep will be scattered), and a closing covenant exchange in balanced lines: God says they are his people, and they say the LORD is their God. The chapter moves from cleansing to judgment to renewed relationship, and the fire of verse 9 answers the fountain of verse 1: water washes, fire refines, and both purify.

outline.t: A fountain for sin and impurity
Idols and false prophets removed from the land
A remnant refined and restored in covenant

doctrines.note: The cleansing of verse 1 is God's provision, not Israel's achievement, and it comes right after the people look on the one they pierced. Sin is treated as a stain needing washing, and God opens the source himself.

The chapter takes false prophecy with deadly seriousness. To speak lies in the LORD's name is not a small religious error; it corrupts the channel by which God guides his people, and the promised future is one in which that corruption is gone.
Verse 9 closes with the classic covenant formula, God claiming a people and the people confessing their God. Judgment is not the end; it is the fire through which the covenant is renewed.

words.note: Maqor, fountain or spring. Jeremiah twice calls the LORD himself the fountain of living water whom Israel abandoned (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13). Here the fountain is opened for a new purpose, to wash away sin, which pairs naturally with the living water that flows from Jerusalem in 14:8.

Ra'ah, to shepherd or pasture, here as the participle, the one who shepherds. Across the ancient Near East kings were called shepherds, and Zechariah 9 to 11 uses the image for Israel's rulers. The striking of the shepherd in verse 7 is the climax of that theme: this time the blow comes by God's own command.

Amit, companion or associate. Outside Zechariah the word appears only in Leviticus, where it means a fellow Israelite, a neighbor on equal footing. Calling the shepherd the man who is My Companion gives him an unusual closeness to God, which is why Christian readers have seen more here than a merely human king.

Tsaraph, to refine or smelt. The metalworker heats ore until the dross separates from the silver or gold. The image is used for God's testing of his people in Isaiah 48:10 and Malachi 3:3; it speaks of suffering that purifies rather than destroys.

christ: Jesus quoted verse 7 on the night of his arrest, telling his disciples that they would all fall away: “I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matthew 26:31; compare Mark 14:27). Within hours they did. The New Testament thus reads the struck shepherd as Jesus, and the detail that the sword is summoned by God himself matches its conviction that the cross happened by God's set purpose, not merely by Roman and priestly hostility. The fountain opened for sin sits beside the pierced one of 12:10, which John applies to the crucifixion (John 19:37), and Christians have long seen in that pairing the cleansing that flows from Christ's death (1 John 1:7 speaks of his blood cleansing from all sin). Verse 6 is sometimes read as a picture of Christ's wounds received from his friends, but in context the speaker is a disowned false prophet, and that reading does not hold.

hard.q: Does verse 3 really command parents to kill their own child for false prophecy?
hard.a: The verse applies the law of Deuteronomy 13 and 18, and on its surface it pictures exactly that. Readers respond in a few ways. Many interpreters take it as prophetic hyperbole: the point is that in God's future, loyalty to the truth will run so deep that even the closest bond will not shelter a lie spoken in God's name, and the next verses show the result, prophets so ashamed they deny ever having been one. Others read it as a description of the covenant law being taken seriously at last, within Israel's theocratic setting, not a rule for families in any other time. Christians also note that the New Testament handles false teaching by exposure, discipline, and exclusion from the church (Matthew 7:15-20; Titus 3:10), never by violence. Across these readings, the chapter treats lying in God's name as among the gravest of sins.

questions: The fountain in verse 1 comes after the mourning of chapter 12. Why might honest grief over sin come before the experience of being cleansed?
False prophets in this chapter trade on appearances (the hairy cloak) and deny who they are when caught. What makes religious speech trustworthy or untrustworthy to you?
Verse 9 describes being refined like silver. Where have hard seasons purified rather than destroyed your faith, and where do they still feel only like fire?
